## Introduction

This assignment uses the `ggplot2` package to draw graphs with the following functions:

`geom_bar()`, `geom_boxplot()`, `geom_density()`, `geom_histogram()`, `geom_hline()`, `geom_jitter()`, `geom_violin()`, `geom_text()`, `geom_smooth()`, `geom_line()`, `geom_point()`, `geom_rug()` and `geom_vline()`.

## How ggplot2 works

Every graph is built in layers:

1. `ggplot(data, aes(x, y))` gives the data and says which variables go on each axis.
2. A `geom_` function adds the shape (bars, points, lines, boxes).
3. More layers can be added with `+` (titles, lines, labels).

## Packages

```{r, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("ggplot2")
```

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(lattice)   # comes with R and contains the singer data
```

## Data

Three datasets that come with R are used, so no files are needed.

```{r}
data(singer)       # height of 235 singers and their voice part
head(singer)
str(singer)
summary(singer)
```

```{r}
data(mtcars)       # fuel consumption and design of 32 cars
head(mtcars[, c("mpg", "wt", "hp", "cyl")])
```

```{r}
data(economics)    # monthly US economic data, from ggplot2
head(economics[, c("date", "unemploy")])
```

## 1. geom_bar()

A bar chart counts how many observations fall in each category. Here: number of singers in each voice part.

```{r}
ggplot(singer, aes(x = voice.part)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Number of singers by voice part", x = "Voice part", y = "Count")
```

## 2. geom_histogram()

A histogram shows the distribution of a continuous variable.

```{r}
ggplot(singer, aes(x = height)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  labs(title = "Height of singers", x = "Height (inches)", y = "Count")
```

## 3. geom_density()

A density plot is a smooth version of the histogram. Filling by voice part compares the groups.

```{r}
ggplot(singer, aes(x = height, fill = voice.part)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(title = "Height distribution by voice part", x = "Height (inches)")
```

## 4. geom_vline()

`geom_vline()` adds a vertical line. Here it marks the mean height on the histogram.

```{r}
ggplot(singer, aes(x = height)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(singer$height), colour = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Height of singers with the mean (red line)", x = "Height (inches)")
```

## 5. geom_rug()

`geom_rug()` draws a small tick for every observation along the axis, so the real data points are visible under the density curve.

```{r}
ggplot(singer, aes(x = height)) +
  geom_density(fill = "lightblue") +
  geom_rug() +
  labs(title = "Density of height with rug", x = "Height (inches)")
```

## 6. geom_boxplot()

A boxplot compares a continuous variable across categories, the same as `boxplot()` in base R.

```{r}
ggplot(singer, aes(x = voice.part, y = height)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  labs(title = "Height by voice part", x = "Voice part", y = "Height (inches)")
```

Lower voices (Bass, Tenor) are taller than higher voices (Alto, Soprano).

## 7. geom_violin()

A violin plot works like a boxplot but shows the full shape of the distribution.

```{r}
ggplot(singer, aes(x = voice.part, y = height)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "lightgreen") +
  labs(title = "Height by voice part (violin)", x = "Voice part", y = "Height (inches)")
```

## 8. geom_jitter()

`geom_jitter()` draws each singer as a point and moves the points slightly sideways so they do not overlap.

```{r}
ggplot(singer, aes(x = voice.part, y = height)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.5, colour = "darkblue") +
  labs(title = "Height by voice part with every singer shown",
       x = "Voice part", y = "Height (inches)")
```

## 9. geom_point()

A scatter plot shows the relationship between two continuous variables, the same as `plot()` in base R.

```{r}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point(colour = "darkblue", size = 2) +
  labs(title = "Car weight and fuel consumption",
       x = "Weight (1000 lbs)", y = "Miles per gallon")
```

## 10. geom_smooth()

`geom_smooth(method = "lm")` adds the linear regression line, the same as `abline(lm())` in base R.

```{r}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "red") +
  labs(title = "Car weight and fuel consumption with regression line",
       x = "Weight (1000 lbs)", y = "Miles per gallon")
cor(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)
```

Heavier cars use more fuel (fewer miles per gallon).

## 11. geom_text()

`geom_text()` writes labels on the graph. Here each point shows the car name.

```{r, fig.height = 6}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, label = rownames(mtcars))) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text(size = 2.5, vjust = -0.7) +
  labs(title = "Car names on the scatter plot",
       x = "Weight (1000 lbs)", y = "Miles per gallon")
```

## 12. geom_hline()

`geom_hline()` adds a horizontal line. Here it marks the average fuel consumption, so cars above the line are more efficient than average.

```{r}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = hp, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(mtcars$mpg), colour = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Horsepower and fuel consumption (red line = mean mpg)",
       x = "Horsepower", y = "Miles per gallon")
```

## 13. geom_line()

`geom_line()` joins the points in order, which suits data over time.

```{r}
ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy / 1000)) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Unemployment in the USA over time",
       x = "Year", y = "Unemployed (millions)")
```

## Combining several geoms

Many functions can be added to one graph. This one uses `geom_point()`, `geom_smooth()`, `geom_hline()`, `geom_vline()` and `geom_rug()` together, with colour by number of cylinders.

```{r}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, colour = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(mtcars$mpg), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(mtcars$wt), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_rug() +
  labs(title = "Weight and fuel consumption by number of cylinders",
       x = "Weight (1000 lbs)", y = "Miles per gallon", colour = "Cylinders")
```

## Conclusion

`ggplot2` builds graphs in layers. The data and axes are set once in `ggplot()`, then each `geom_` function adds a different view: `geom_bar()` for counts, `geom_histogram()`, `geom_density()` and `geom_rug()` for distributions, `geom_boxplot()`, `geom_violin()` and `geom_jitter()` to compare groups, `geom_point()`, `geom_smooth()` and `geom_text()` for relationships, `geom_line()` for time, and `geom_hline()` and `geom_vline()` for reference lines.
